At the Monday stand-up in the Pune office, Chinmay raised his hand. “If the festival sale traffic doubles like last year, our servers will crash. We haven't load-tested.”
Francis, the team lead, smiled thinly. “Chinmay, you always find the problem. Can we be team players for once?” Somebody laughed. Two others nodded at Francis.
Chinmay said, “Sure,” and looked at his laptop.
He didn't raise his hand at the next four meetings. At lunch he scrolled old photos from his first year, when the whole team used to argue loudly over pizza and it had felt like a family.
On sale day the site went down for forty minutes. Nobody mentioned his warning. That evening he updated his CV.

qa.q: How long did the site go down on sale day?
qa.a: The site went down for forty minutes.

qa.q: How did Chinmay feel looking at old photos at lunch?
qa.a: He felt nostalgic and lonely, missing the days when the team argued openly and still felt like a family.

qa.q: What could Francis have done when Chinmay raised the risk?
qa.a: Francis could have thanked him and asked the team to check the load-testing, instead of calling the warning un-teamlike.

qa.q: How might the colleagues who nodded at Francis see things after sale day?
qa.a: They might feel awkward and a little guilty, realising the person they laughed at was right.

grounding: Shows a team member who raises a risk being called not a team player, going quiet and preparing to leave.

subtopic: Groupthink
passage:
Rukhsar, you're worried your team argues too much? Sit. This is Leela, your old senior, with a story from when I first managed a team.
I was twenty-five, at the publishing house. My meetings were beautiful. I proposed; everyone agreed. I went home proud every week.

The next meeting, I asked, “Tell me what's wrong with this plan.” Silence, then one voice, then five. We found two big mistakes before print.

Diwali week at the Chandigarh restaurant, and orders were double. Dilnaz, the young kitchen manager, held the staff meeting standing by the walk-in fridge, ten minutes before service.
“New menu tonight. Any problems?” Seven heads shook. Done in ninety seconds.

Dilnaz called the gas mechanic at once and moved that dish to another burner. Then she told everyone: “If something's wrong, I want to hear it. Always.”

qa.a: He probably felt hesitant but relieved, since the last manager had told the staff to stop complaining.

subtopic: Groupthink
passage:
In a small design studio in Osaka, Layla pinned the new café logo on the wall. Everyone loved it. Kenji clapped. Mariko said, “Perfect.”
Layla held up a hand. “Aiko, would you do me a favour? Argue against it. Pretend you hate it. Give me three reasons.”
Aiko laughed, surprised, then took it seriously. “It's hard to read from across the street. Red looks like a warning. And it's a lot like the bakery next door.”
Nobody spoke for a moment. Then Kenji said, “The bakery thing is true.”
Layla spoke last. “Thank you, Aiko. That's exactly why I asked.” She changed the colour and the font that week. The café owner said, “Now I can see it from the station.”

qa.a: She asked someone to argue against the plan, spoke last herself, and thanked Aiko openly for raising problems.

qa.q: How might Kenji and Mariko have felt after Aiko's points?
qa.a: They may have felt a little embarrassed at first, then glad the flaws were caught before the café owner saw them.

grounding: Shows a lead who asks someone to argue against a popular plan, speaks last and thanks the critic, making dissent normal.

subtopic: Groupthink
passage:
The school timetable committee met in the staffroom after last bell. Tejas, the youngest head of department, had drafted a new timetable. Everyone seemed ready to sign.
“Before anyone says yes,” Tejas said, “Parveen ma'am, would you be our devil's advocate today? Find everything wrong with it.”
Parveen raised an eyebrow, then smiled. “Happily. Grade 6 has maths in the last period four days a week. They'll be asleep. And the lab is double-booked on Thursdays.”
Two teachers laughed in surprise. One said, “She's right about Thursdays.”
Tejas waited until everyone had spoken. Then he said, “Thank you, Parveen ma'am. Let's rotate the role every meeting.” The committee fixed both problems before the new term.

qa.a: They won't be stuck with tired last-period maths four days a week, so their learning is likely to be better.

At recess in the village school at Chitrakoot, Anirban fell off the high swing and landed hard on the stones. He curled up, holding his arm.

qa.a: He was probably in pain and frightened, and it may have felt lonely that so many watched and nobody helped at first.

School counsellor's note, Thursday.
Farida came to see me after lunch, upset. Yesterday at the bus stop, two older boys were shoving Sumit, a Class 9 student, against the railing. A group of about eight was watching.
Farida said she looked around at everyone's faces. They were calm, some even smiling. “So I thought it must be a joke between them,” she said. “Nobody else seemed worried.” Today she heard Sumit has a bruised shoulder and hasn't come to school.

qa.a: The counsellor reassured Farida, informed the vice-principal and called Sumit's parents the same afternoon, so Sumit gets support quickly.

qa.a: Sumit probably felt scared and alone, seeing nobody step in during the shoving.

I'm Tushar, and there's a metro ride last winter I think about a lot.
It was packed. Mahima from my tuition was standing near the door. A man kept pressing closer to her, and she was leaning away, holding her bag in front of her. Her face looked stiff.

An aunty next to her finally said loudly, “Bhai sahab, step back!” He got off at the next station.
Mahima didn't look at me. That night I couldn't sleep. I had been scared of looking foolish, and she had been scared, full stop.

qa.a: Tushar could have moved to stand between them, or asked Mahima, "Want to swap places?", which helps without needing to be sure.

qa.q: How might Mahima have felt during the ride?
qa.a: She likely felt frightened and trapped, leaning away and holding her bag, and hurt that people she knew stayed silent.

Teacher's note, school fair duty, Saturday.
Around four, a small boy was crying by the ring-toss stall, clearly lost. Dolma, from Class 10, was at the next stall with Rafiq and three others. She told me later she saw him for several minutes.
